How well did the transport network survive the flood — ward by ward?

The Historical Transport Resilience Index (TRI) reconstructs, from observed-style road, flood, facility and travel-survey data, exactly what happened to a city's transport system during a historical flood event: which roads stayed open, which essential services people could still reach, and how travellers actually adapted.

1 What this is

A retrospective resilience audit, not a prediction

Every number on this site describes what already happened during one historical flood event. There is no machine learning, no forecasting, and no what-if simulation anywhere in the pipeline — every score is a transparent, auditable calculation over real (here: synthetically generated for demonstration) spatial and survey data.

✓  Road–flood overlay, network graph analysis, survey aggregation
✓  Transparent, rule-based formulas — every step is auditable
✓  Fully reproducible: one run_pipeline() call, files on disk at every stage
✗  No machine learning or deep learning models
✗  No predictive or forecasting components
✗  No LLMs, RAG, or generative-AI components anywhere

2 File Formats

Formats used across the pipeline

.shp / .dbf / .shx / .prj / .cpg

ESRI Shapefile bundle — vector geometry (roads, boundary, facilities). Field names are capped at 10 characters.

.tif (GeoTIFF)

Single-band Float32 raster — flood inundation depth, 10 × 10 m resolution, nodata = −9999.

.csv

Tabular data — travel survey inputs and every intermediate / final numeric result (IF, AI, BA, TRI).

.png

Rendered maps and chart outputs — one per pipeline stage, plus a combined contact-sheet overview.

Workflow & Architecture

From raw layers to a single resilience score

Road geometry is overlaid on the flood raster to get an average flood depth per segment. Each segment is classified Operational / Partial / Closed. The surviving network becomes a graph used to test which facilities each ward can still reach. Independently, the travel survey tells us what travellers actually experienced. The three ward-level indices combine into the final TRI.

2 Pipeline

The 10-step run_pipeline() sequence

A single function call executes the entire historical TRI pipeline — dummy data generation through TRI and visualization — with no manual intervention, proving the process is reproducible end to end.

Generate synthetic input data

Creates the 9-ward boundary, road network, flood-depth raster, essential facilities and household travel survey used for this proof of concept.

out: boundary.shp, roads.shp, flood_depth.tif, facilities.shp, travel_survey.csv

Road–Flood Overlay

Zonal statistics compute the average flood inundation depth under each road segment.

in: roads.shp, flood_depth.tifout: road_overlay.shp (+avg_flood)

Road Status Classification

Each segment is labelled by depth threshold: Operational < 0.20 m, Partial 0.20–0.50 m, Closed > 0.50 m.

in: road_overlay.shpout: road_status.shp (+status)

Infrastructure Functionality (IF)

Roads are split by ward boundary; each segment's length is weighted by its status (Operational = 1.0, Partial = 0.5, Closed = 0.0) and summed. IF = effective length ÷ total length × 100.

in: road_status.shp, boundary.shpout: if.csv

Build the surviving road graph

An undirected, length-weighted graph is built from all non-Closed road segments — this is the network people can actually use after the flood.

in: road_status.shpout: in-memory NetworkX graph

Accessibility Index (AI)

For every ward, test whether a path exists from the ward centroid to each essential facility on the surviving graph. AI = reachable facilities ÷ total facilities × 100.

in: road_status.shp, facilities.shp, boundary.shpout: accessibility.csv

Travel Behaviour

Per-trip indicators are derived from the raw survey: delay (after − before travel time), whether the mode changed, whether the trip completed, whether the route changed.

in: travel_survey.csvout: behaviour.csv

Behavioural Adaptation (BA)

Trip-level behaviour is aggregated per ward into three 0–1 sub-scores — completion, delay, and stability — then averaged: BA = (completion_score + delay_score + stability_score) / 3.

in: behaviour.csvout: ba.csv

Master Dataset & TRI

IF, AI and BA are merged on ward_id (BA rescaled ×100 to match IF/AI), then combined: TRI = (IF + AI + BA) / 3, rounded to 2 decimals.

in: if.csv, accessibility.csv, ba.csvout: master_resilience.csv, tri.csv

Visualize & validate

Every vector, raster and CSV product is rendered as a PNG map or chart; a combined contact-sheet overview and a printed end-of-run summary close out the pipeline.

out: output/maps/*.png, printed ward ranking
3 Formulas

Exact calculations used

Road status thresholds

depth < 0.20 m → Operational
0.20 ≤ depth ≤ 0.50 m → Partial
depth > 0.50 m → Closed

Infrastructure Functionality

weights = {Operational:1.0, Partial:0.5, Closed:0.0}
IF = Σ(segment_length × weight) / Σ(segment_length) × 100

Accessibility Index

Graph built from non-Closed roads only.
AI = reachable_facilities / total_facilities × 100 per ward, via shortest-path existence from the ward centroid.

Behavioural Adaptation

completion_score = pct_completed / 100
delay_score = 1 − (avg_delay / max_delay)
stability_score = 1 − (pct_mode_changed + pct_route_changed) / 200
BA = mean(completion, delay, stability), rescaled ×100

Composite Transport Resilience Index

TRI = ( IF + AI + BA ) / 3

4 Reproducibility

Why this pipeline is auditable

Every step writes to disk

Shapefile, GeoTIFF or CSV at each stage — nothing lives only in memory.

Every function is independent

Any stage can be re-run on its own by reading the file the previous stage produced.

One call runs it all

run_pipeline(base_dir) executes every stage from a fresh directory and prints the final ward ranking.

Indicators

What each score means, who computes it, and who acts on it

Four numbers drive every decision this framework supports. Here's what each one actually measures, the roles typically responsible for producing and using it, and what a low score should trigger.

1 IF
IF

Infrastructure Functionality

Can the physical road network carry traffic?
Meaning

The share of a ward's road length that remains usable after the flood, with Partial roads counted at half weight. It answers: “how much of the physical network still works?”

Computed by
  • GIS / transport engineering team
  • Road & Highways authority
  • Inputs: road network + flood raster
Impact of a low score

A severed network blocks emergency vehicles and supply routes regardless of demand. Low-IF wards are priority candidates for drainage works, road raising, or emergency repair crews.

2 AI
AI

Accessibility Index

Can people actually reach essential services?
Meaning

The share of essential facilities (hospitals, schools, markets, transit stops) a ward can still reach through the surviving road graph. A ward can have decent roads and still score low here if the facilities it needs sit outside its reachable network.

Computed by
  • Urban / facility-location planners
  • Health & education departments (as data owners of facility locations)
  • Inputs: road-status graph + facility points
Impact of a low score

Low AI means functional isolation even where roads are intact — the ward is cut off from care, schooling, or supply. Signals for temporary service points, mobile clinics, or targeted access-road repair.

3 BA
BA

Behavioural Adaptation

How did real travellers cope?
Meaning

A blend of trip completion rate, relative delay, and route/mode stability drawn from the household travel survey. It captures the lived experience of disruption that infrastructure and access metrics alone can miss.

Computed by
  • Travel-demand / survey analysts
  • Transit operators & traffic police (as data sources)
  • Inputs: household / traveller survey
Impact of a low score

Low BA means people faced long delays, cancelled trips, or had to change mode or route. Signals for better real-time traveller information, temporary transit services, or traffic management during future events.

4 TRI
Σ

Transport Resilience Index (composite)

The single ward-level resilience score
Meaning

The simple average of IF, AI and BA. A high TRI needs the network, access, and lived experience to all hold up together — a weakness in any one pulls the composite down.

Computed by
  • Resilience / disaster-management program office
  • City GIS & analytics unit (this pipeline)
  • Inputs: IF + AI + BA, merged
Impact of a low score

Used to rank wards for post-event investment, insurance / donor reporting, and to target the specific weak leg (IF, AI, or BA) rather than applying a one-size-fits-all response.

6 Interpretation bands

Suggested TRI reading (0–100 scale)

These bands are an interpretive convenience for this proof of concept, not a fixed standard produced by the notebook itself — adjust them to local policy thresholds before operational use.

TRI ≥ 35

Higher relative resilience

Network, access and traveller experience held up comparatively well.

25 ≤ TRI < 35

Moderate resilience

Partial disruption in at least one indicator; worth monitoring.

TRI < 25

Priority for intervention

Significant weakness in infrastructure, access, or behaviour — investigate the driving sub-indicator.

4 Key findings

What the results show

1

W02 is the most resilient ward (TRI 37.85)

Not the ward with the best roads — its edge comes from the highest Accessibility Index (28.0), reaching 7 of 25 facilities even after the flood.

2

W05 is the least resilient ward (TRI 22.50)

Its road network was completely severed — IF = 0 — dragging its composite score down even though its behavioural adaptation (BA 55.5) was mid-range.

3

Good roads don't guarantee good access

W07 has the highest Infrastructure Functionality (31.84) but the lowest Accessibility Index (8.0) — its surviving roads simply don't lead to where the facilities are.

4

Behavioural Adaptation is the most stable indicator

BA ranges only 52.8–72.0 across wards, compared to IF's 0–31.84 — traveller coping behaviour varied far less than physical infrastructure damage.

5 Conclusion

The composite view changes the priority order

Looking at any single indicator alone would misdirect resources: IF alone would flag W05 and the two lowest-IF wards as worst-off; AI alone would put W07 at the bottom; only the composite TRI reveals that resilience is genuinely multi-dimensional — a ward can lose on infrastructure, on access, or on lived traveller experience, and each failure mode calls for a different response.

Priority 1 — W05, W08, W06: lowest TRI; start with infrastructure repair (IF) since all three show depressed road functionality.
Priority 2 — W07: strong roads but poor access; investigate facility distribution and reroute or relocate services rather than repairing roads.
Maintain — W02, W01: highest TRI; use as a reference pattern for what balanced resilience looks like across IF, AI and BA.
Next step: re-run this exact pipeline on real observed road, flood, facility and survey data from an actual event to replace the synthetic inputs with an operational assessment.
